common_name: Allahabad Safeda Guava (Classic Indian White-Fleshed Guava)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained soil; in zone 9a grow in a large pot that can be sheltered or in the warmest, most protected microclimate available, since this is a tender tropical guava selection with no special cold hardiness bred in.

directions: Allahabad Safeda is one of India's best-known commercial guava cultivars, grown around the city of Allahabad (Prayagraj) for its smooth, round, pale-skinned fruit and soft, creamy white, sweetly aromatic flesh with relatively few seeds. It is primarily a fresh-eating cultivar prized for long shelf life and good shipping quality compared to many seedling guavas. On the Gulf Coast this is a tender, purely tropical selection rather than a cold-hardy one, so zone 9a growers should plan on large container culture with winter shelter, or a south-facing wall microclimate with heavy trunk wrapping and mulching during cold snaps. Guava fruits on new wood, so an annual late-winter prune after the coldest weather has passed keeps a container-grown plant compact and encourages a strong flush of fruiting growth each season.
sources: National Horticulture Board (India) — Guava Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Guava Growing in the Home Landscape
California Rare Fruit Growers

common_name: Hong Kong Pink Guava (Pink-Fleshed Hawaiian-Bred Guava)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown tree in spring after frost risk passes, in full sun with well-drained soil; in zone 9a this tender tropical guava is best grown in a large pot moved under cover for winter, since it has no particular cold tolerance beyond that typical of common guava.

directions: Hong Kong Pink was selected from seed of a Hong Kong guava cultivar at the University of Hawaii's Poamoho Research Station, and is grown for its medium to large, roundish fruit with thin, smooth skin and pink-red flesh that is subacid to sweet with relatively few seeds. It bears young and heavily, making it a satisfying choice for a first guava in a Gulf Coast dooryard or large container. Because it carries no special frost tolerance, zone 9a gardeners should treat it as container stock to be moved into a garage, greenhouse, or heavily insulated spot whenever temperatures threaten to dip near or below freezing. Keep the root zone heavily mulched and prune lightly each late winter to shape the plant and stimulate the new growth that carries the next flush of fruit.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR — Guava Cultivar Notes
Specialty Produce — Hong Kong Pink Guava Profile

common_name: Hortus Gold Papaya (South African Golden-Fleshed Papaya)

planting.note: Start seed indoors and transplant outside 2-6 weeks after the last frost once soil and nights are reliably warm; papaya is a fast-growing, short-lived tropical that in zone 9a is typically treated as an annual or grown in a large container that can be moved indoors for winter.

directions: Hortus Gold is a South African papaya cultivar released in the early 1950s from selections made at the University of Natal, valued for its early maturity, high sugar content, and disease resistance. It bears round-oval, golden-yellow fruit with yellow flesh that is roughly twice the size of Hawaiian Solo-type papayas, giving a bigger harvest per fruit for home growers. Because papaya has essentially no cold tolerance, zone 9a growers should plant it in spring as a fast-fruiting warm-season crop, or keep it in a large container that can be moved to a frost-free location in winter, since even a light freeze will kill the soft trunk and foliage. Papaya plants are naturally short-lived (often most productive in their first two to three years), so many Gulf Coast growers simply replant from seed each year rather than trying to overwinter mature trees.
sources: University of Natal / Fruit Facts — Hortus Gold Papaya
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Papaya Profile (Julia Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates)

common_name: Sunrise Solo Papaya (Strawberry Papaya, Red-Fleshed Hawaiian Solo)

planting.note: Start seed indoors and transplant outside 2-6 weeks after the last frost once nights stay reliably warm; this compact, precocious Solo-type papaya is well suited to large container culture in zone 9a since it fruits low on the trunk at only about 3 feet of height.

directions: Sunrise Solo was bred at the University of Hawaii in 1961, crossing an orange-red-fleshed breeding line with the high-quality Kariya Solo strain to produce a precocious, pear-shaped papaya with vivid reddish-orange flesh and a notably sweet flavor, widely sold fresh under the nickname strawberry papaya. It is more compact and bears lower on the trunk than many papaya cultivars, which makes it one of the more practical choices for growing in a large container on the Gulf Coast. Papaya has no frost tolerance at all, so zone 9a gardeners should either grow it as a warm-season annual started fresh from seed each spring, or keep container specimens ready to move under cover whenever a freeze threatens. Because papaya can be dioecious or produce bisexual flowers depending on the seed line, growing a few seedlings together improves the odds of good fruit set.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR — 'Sunrise Solo': A Different Colored Solo Papaya
Hawaii Papaya Industry Association — Papaya Choices
Purdue University Center for New Crops — Papaya Profile

common_name: Burtons Favourite Cherimoya (Bushy Cool-Climate New Zealand Cherimoya)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained soil; in zone 9a grow in a large container that can be sheltered, or in a warm, wind-protected microclimate, since cherimoya wood is damaged by hard freezes.

directions: Burtons Favourite is a New Zealand-bred cherimoya selection grown on a medium-sized, naturally bushy tree with soft, velvety-undersided leaves, prized for performing relatively well in cooler, marginal cherimoya climates. Its moderate-to-large, heart-shaped, knobby green fruit carries creamy white, delicately sweet flesh often compared to custard in both flavor and texture, best eaten fresh with a spoon once the fruit has softened at room temperature after picking. Cherimoya flowers are notoriously poor at self-pollinating because their male and female parts mature at different times, so hand pollination with a small brush in early morning greatly improves fruit set, especially on an isolated container specimen. In zone 9a, Burtons Favourite is best grown as a large container plant that can be moved to a garage or greenhouse during freezes, since the tree tolerates only brief, light chilling and hard frost kills young wood outright.
sources: Wikipedia — List of Cherimoya Cultivars
Flying Dragon Nursery (NZ) — Cherimoya 'Burtons Favourite'

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained soil; in zone 9a El Bumpo is best grown as a large container specimen that can be sheltered from freezes, since it was bred for mild California conditions rather than cold tolerance.

directions: El Bumpo was selected by grower Rudy Haluza in Villa Park, California in 1986 and takes its name from the large, pronounced bumps (mammillations) covering its conical, medium-to-large fruit. The thin, nearly edible skin covers very soft, creamy flesh with a rich flavor often described as combining banana, pineapple, and pear, placing it among the best-flavored cherimoya selections grown by home enthusiasts rather than commercial growers. Like other cherimoyas, flowers rarely self-pollinate well because the male and female flower parts are not receptive at the same time, so hand pollination with a soft brush in early morning substantially improves fruit set. In zone 9a, grow El Bumpo in a large container that can be moved to shelter during freezes, since the tree is sensitive to hard frost and the very soft-skinned fruit bruises easily, so handle ripening fruit gently and harvest just as it begins to soften.
sources: Wikipedia — List of Cherimoya Cultivars
California Rare Fruit Growers — Cherimoya

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained soil; in zone 9a grow in a large container that can be sheltered, since Lisa inherits only moderate cold tolerance from its cherimoya parentage and hard freezes will damage or kill the top growth.

directions: Lisa is a Florida-bred atemoya created in the 1990s by hobby breeder Har Mahdeem, who crossed a 'Libby' cherimoya flower with pollen from a red-skinned sugar apple selection; the cross gives Lisa its signature pink-blushed skin and a juicy, distinctly berry-like flavor that sets it apart from the more custardy flavor typical of most atemoya cultivars. Fruit ripens in late summer to early fall and is ready to pick once it softens slightly and develops a strong, sweet aroma. Because Lisa carries some cherimoya parentage, its root system has somewhat better cold tolerance than a pure sugar apple, but the tree is not reliably self-fertile and benefits from hand pollination with a small brush in the early morning when flowers are receptive. In zone 9a, treat Lisa as container stock moved under cover during freezes, or plant in the most frost-protected microclimate available and expect dieback after a hard winter.
sources: MiamiFruit.org — Lisa Atemoya Cultivar Notes

common_name: Balanagar Sugar Apple (India's Leading Custard Apple Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or container-grown tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained soil; in zone 9a this is a fully tropical selection best grown in a large container that can be sheltered from any frost.

directions: Balanagar is the most widely grown sugar apple cultivar in India, prized by growers for its reliable, high yields and adaptability across a range of growing conditions. Fruit is medium-sized with green skin and the classic knobby, segmented surface of sugar apple, ripening during the late-summer rainy season and giving sweet, grainy, custard-like flesh once the fruit softens fully. Sugar apple tolerates less cold than its cherimoya relatives and has essentially no frost hardiness, so in zone 9a it should be grown strictly as a container specimen moved to full shelter whenever temperatures approach freezing. Prune lightly after the coldest part of winter to remove any frost-damaged wood and shape the tree, since fruit forms on new growth produced each season.
sources: Journal of Horticultural Sciences (India) — Balanagar Sugar Apple Cultivar Studies

common_name: Neitzel Dragon Fruit (Classic Self-Fertile White-Fleshed Pitaya)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after all frost danger has passed, giving the climbing cactus a sturdy post or trellis for support; in zone 9a grow in a large container that can be moved to shelter during freezes, since the succulent stems are easily damaged by frost.

directions: Neitzel is a long-established white-fleshed dragon fruit selection popularized by California rare fruit growers, valued for its self-fertile flowers that reliably set fruit without hand pollination, unlike many dragon fruit cultivars. Fruit can reach up to a pound, with sweet, mild white flesh that many growers find best when chilled before eating. Neitzel has also been an important parent in modern dragon fruit breeding, contributing to well-known hybrids such as Purple Haze and Physical Graffiti. As an epiphytic cactus, it needs very well-drained, sandy to loamy soil and infrequent deep watering rather than regular irrigation; in zone 9a, container culture with winter shelter is the most reliable approach, since the fleshy stems and shallow roots have little tolerance for hard freezes.
sources: Pine Island Nursery — Neitzel Dragon Fruit Variety Notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dragon Fruit Production in Florida

common_name: Cosmic Charlie Dragon Fruit (Grape-Flavored Purple-Fleshed Pitaya)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after all frost danger has passed, providing a sturdy post or trellis for the climbing cactus stems; in zone 9a grow in a large container that can be sheltered from freezes, and plan to hand-pollinate at night since fruit set on this hybrid can be inconsistent without it.

directions: Cosmic Charlie is a dragon fruit hybrid bred by noted fruit breeder Paul Thomson from a cross between the purple-fleshed Rixford and the white-fleshed Neitzel, producing large, pound-to-pound-and-a-half fruit with deep purple flesh and a rich, grape-like flavor unlike the milder taste of most white-fleshed pitaya. The plant grows as a medium, somewhat bushy climbing cactus with fast-growing, three-angled stems. Reports on self-fertility are mixed — some growers get fruit without help while others find hand pollination at night necessary for a reliable crop, so keeping a second dragon fruit cultivar nearby as a pollen source is good insurance. In zone 9a, grow Cosmic Charlie in a large container with very well-drained, sandy soil that can be moved under cover during freezes, since like all dragon fruit it has essentially no frost tolerance in its succulent stems.
sources: Top Tropicals — Cosmic Charlie Dragon Fruit
Spicy Exotics — Cosmic Charlie Dragon Fruit Profile

common_name: Pina Colada Mango (Ultra-Dwarf Condo Mango with Tropical Candy Flavor)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Pina Colada is a true condo-type dwarf mango bred to stay compact with annual pruning, making it one of the more practical mango choices for zone 9a container culture.

directions: Pina Colada was developed in Boynton Beach, Florida by mango breeder Gary Zill as a seedling of 'Dot' pollinated by 'Gary', and released around 2012 as one of the most compact condo-type mangoes available, with a naturally low-vigor, dense canopy that can realistically be kept to 6-10 feet with annual pruning. The small, half-to-three-quarter-pound fruit is fiberless and intensely aromatic, with a flavor reminiscent of its namesake drink, combining pineapple, coconut, and tropical candy notes rather than the straightforward sweetness of most mango cultivars. Its compact size makes Pina Colada a strong candidate for growing in a large pot on the Gulf Coast, where it can be moved to shelter whenever a freeze threatens, since mango wood has no frost tolerance at all. Reduce irrigation as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate flavor and sugars, and prune immediately after harvest to maintain the compact habit the cultivar was bred for.
sources: Mango.org (National Mango Board) — Zill Mango Cultivar Descriptions
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mangifera indica 'Pina Colada'
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Home Landscape

common_name: Coconut Cream Mango (Semi-Dwarf Container Mango with Coconut Flavor)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil, or grow in a large container to shelter from frost; Coconut Cream is a semi-dwarf selection that can be kept to 10-15 feet with regular pruning, making it workable for a large patio pot or protected Gulf Coast planting site.

directions: Coconut Cream was bred by Walter Zill in Boynton Beach, Florida, likely from Edward mango parentage, and produces medium-to-large, 12-16 ounce fruit with creamy, fiberless flesh carrying a distinctive coconut flavor that sets it apart from typical mango cultivars. The tree has a semi-dwarf, somewhat lanky and twisted growth habit that responds well to pruning, generally staying manageable at 10-15 feet rather than growing into a full-sized mango tree. Because mango wood has no frost tolerance, zone 9a gardeners should grow Coconut Cream in a large container that can be moved under cover during freezes, or reserve it for the warmest, most sheltered microclimate available and accept some risk of cold damage in a hard winter. Reduce watering as fruit matures to concentrate sugars and flavor, and harvest when fruit develops a slight give and full aroma.
sources: Mango.org (National Mango Board) — Zill Mango Cultivar Descriptions

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained, acidic soil; in zone 9a grow in a large container that can be sheltered, or in the warmest protected microclimate available, since lychee wood is damaged by hard freezes.

directions: Salathiel, also known as Lou Mai Chee, is an Australian-grown lychee cultivar valued for bright red, smooth-skinned fruit with a very small chicken-tongue seed, meaning most of the fruit is solid, flavorful aril. It is noted among lychee growers for setting fruit more consistently than many other cultivars and for good eating quality, with fruit typically ready in early summer. Salathiel tends to perform well in cooler, more marginal subtropical lychee climates compared to some tropical cultivars, which makes it worth trying at the northern edge of lychee range, though it still has no real frost tolerance. In zone 9a, grow Salathiel in a large container that can be moved to shelter during freezes, or in acidic, well-drained soil in a wind-protected, south-facing spot, and mulch the root zone heavily each winter since lychee roots are sensitive to cold, wet soil as well as to frost.
sources: Australian Lychee Growers' Association — Salathiel Variety Notes
Daley's Fruit Tree Nursery (Australia) — Lychee Salathiel

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained soil; in zone 9a grow in a large container that can be sheltered, since longan has only slightly more cold tolerance than lychee and young wood is still damaged by hard freezes.

directions: Edau, also written E-Daw or Daw, is historically the most widely planted longan cultivar in Thailand, prized by growers for consistent, heavy yields of medium-to-large fruit with a sweet, crisp, clean-flavored aril. It has been introduced to Florida alongside other Thai cultivars such as Chompoo and Haew for evaluation alongside the industry-standard Kohala, though Kohala remains more widely planted there. Edau has shown some pollination and fruit-set difficulties in subtropical conditions outside its native tropical range, so growing it alongside another longan cultivar can help ensure a reliable crop. In zone 9a, treat Edau as container stock moved to shelter during freezes, or plant in the warmest, most wind-protected site available, since longan wood tolerates only brief, light chilling and is killed back by hard frost.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — The Longan in Florida

common_name: B10 Carambola (Malaysia's Leading Commercial Sweet Starfruit)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in full sun with well-drained soil; in zone 9a grow in a large container that can be sheltered, since carambola is a fully tropical tree with no meaningful frost tolerance.

directions: B10 has been Malaysia's most popular commercial carambola clone for decades, grown for its large, oval, gold-yellow fruit with sweet, aromatic, fine-textured flesh and relatively high sugar content compared to older starfruit selections. The tree is naturally small with attractive pink flowers and somewhat weeping branches, which keeps it reasonably manageable in a home garden or large container. B10 has short-styled flowers, so fruit set and yield improve markedly when a long-styled pollinator cultivar is planted nearby. In zone 9a, grow B10 in a large container that can be moved under cover during freezes, or in the warmest, most sheltered site available, since carambola wood has no cold hardiness and even a light frost damages young growth; established plants may resprout from larger wood after a mild freeze but should be protected whenever possible.
sources: International Tropical Fruits Network — Malaysian Carambola: From a Rising Star to a Global Leader
